header_title: The Falling Elevator Is the Universe
tagline: Weight and gravity are locally indistinguishable
question_text: Why can no experiment tell free fall from deep space?
audio_script: I am going to show you the thought experiment Einstein called his happiest. You are standing on a bathroom scale inside an elevator. The cable snaps. The elevator falls. In the first instant, the scale reads your weight. A fraction of a second later, it reads less. Then less. Then zero. What happened? Your mass did not change. Gravity still pulls on you exactly the same way. But you and the scale are both accelerating downward at g. There is no normal force left for the scale to measure. It reads zero because it has nothing to push against. Here is the strange part, and it is the seed of general relativity. The exact same scale reading, zero, could also be produced by removing you and the scale to deep space, far from any planet or star, and letting the whole apparatus drift. Free fall and weightlessness are locally indistinguishable. No experiment you can perform inside that falling room can tell you which one you are in. A pendulum hangs straight. A laser beam travels in a straight line. A dropped ball floats next to you. Every physical test gives the same answer. The word is local. If your body were the size of a planet, you could measure the tidal pull across your width. The top of your head would fall at a slightly different rate than your toes, and you would feel a stretching force. But for a small room in free fall, the physics inside is exactly the physics of empty space. This is why astronauts float on the space station. They are not far from Earth's gravity. They are falling around it, forever missing the ground. Inside their little falling room, no experiment can tell them whether they are at rest in the void or crashing toward a planet.

tagline: Every explosion has a still center
question_text: Where is the center of a spinning exploding object?
audio_script: I am going to show you a point that does not know an explosion has happened. Light a firework. It climbs. At the top of its arc it explodes into a hundred fragments. Every fragment flies off in its own direction. Every fragment follows its own parabola. The motion looks chaotic. Now watch a single point. The center of mass. Follow it through the explosion. It continues along exactly the same smooth path it would have followed if the firework had never exploded. It does not know the shell broke apart. It does not know a hundred pieces are flying. It keeps moving as if nothing happened. This is the deepest structural fact about many-body physics. Newton's second law applied to every atom separately is a nightmare of bookkeeping. Applied once to the center of mass, it becomes a single sentence. The net external force equals total mass times the acceleration of the center of mass. Internal forces cancel in pairs. They never move the center of mass. This is why a bullet and a rifle recoil together. Why a rocket accelerates even though the exhaust is pushing away from it. Why two ice skaters who push off each end up with the same center of mass they started with. A hundred particles, a thousand, a billion. The center of mass always behaves like a single particle carrying all the mass, driven only by the net external force. Every explosion has a still point. The center of mass knows nothing of chaos.

tagline: Mass distribution sets the race
question_text: A hoop and a disk roll down the same ramp. Which wins?
audio_script: I am going to show you why the disk always wins. Take a hoop and a solid disk. Same mass. Same radius. Put them at the top of the same ramp. Release. The disk reaches the bottom first. Every time. You have probably seen this experiment and never thought carefully about why. Both objects lose exactly the same amount of potential energy on the way down. Both end up with exactly the same total kinetic energy. So why does one finish first? Because kinetic energy comes in two flavours. Translational, one half m v squared. Rotational, one half I omega squared. For rolling without slipping, v equals omega R. So the rotational share depends only on the moment of inertia. The hoop's mass sits at the rim, far from the axis. Its moment of inertia is m R squared. The disk's mass is spread out, with much of it closer to the axis. Its moment of inertia is only one half m R squared. A bigger fraction of the hoop's kinetic energy goes into spinning. Less is left for rolling forward. The hoop loses the race. The same physics explains why a solid sphere beats a hollow sphere, and why a can of soup rolls faster than an empty can. It is not the mass that matters. It is where the mass lives. Every flywheel ever designed leans on this one fact. You put the mass at the rim on purpose, to store rotational energy, or you pull it toward the centre, to move faster.

tagline: A pendulum's period depends only on length
question_text: Why does the swing rhythm stay the same at every size?
audio_script: I am going to show you something that surprised Galileo. Watch a grandfather clock. The pendulum swings back and forth, back and forth, at the same tempo, hour after hour. The clock keeps time. Now watch closely as the clock runs down. The swing gets smaller. The bob travels a shorter and shorter arc. Yet the period does not change. A small swing and a large swing take exactly the same time. This is strange. Think about it from the pendulum's point of view. A large swing means the bob moves farther. You would expect it to take longer. But it does not. Why? Look at the forces. The restoring force on the bob comes from gravity pulling it back toward the bottom of the arc. For small angles, that force is proportional to the displacement. Double the displacement, double the force. That linearity is what makes the motion simple harmonic, and it is what makes the period independent of amplitude. It is called isochronism. Galileo noticed it as a young man watching a chandelier sway in a cathedral in Pisa. He timed it against his own pulse, because that was the only clock he had. The period depends only on the length of the pendulum and on g. Not on the mass of the bob. Not on the amplitude, as long as the angle stays small. Shorten the string, and the clock runs fast. Move it to the Moon, where g is smaller, and it runs slow. A one meter pendulum has a period of about two seconds. Cut it to a quarter of a meter, and the period halves to one second. Everything about the motion scales, but the rhythm stays pure.

header_title: A Wave Is Not the Medium
tagline: The pattern travels while the particles stay put
question_text: Does the string travel with the wave?
audio_script: I am going to show you one of the most confusing ideas in wave physics. Pluck a guitar string. A wave travels from one end to the other. That is obvious. But now watch a single point on the string. Mark it with a small dot of paint and watch it as the wave passes by. The point moves up and down. It does not travel with the wave. It stays at its position along the string. When the wave arrives, the point rises, falls, rises again. When the wave leaves, the point is back where it started. Nothing has moved except the disturbance. This is the central insight. The wave is the pattern. The medium oscillates in place. If you take a snapshot of the wave at any instant, you see a shape. A fraction of a second later, the shape has shifted. But the particles of the medium have not. They have only bobbed in place. The wave is the message. The medium is just the messenger. On a string, the wave speed is the square root of tension over linear density. Tighten the string, and the wave speeds up. Make it heavier, and the wave slows down. This is why thick bass strings play low notes on a guitar. Slower wave, longer wavelength, lower pitch. And it is why the same note on a violin and a cello sounds different. Same wave, different medium. Every vibration of every atom in your body, every photon arriving from the Sun, every ocean swell rolling into a shore obeys this same distinction.

header_title: Blow Across a Sheet of Paper
tagline: Fast air pushes less. You would have guessed more.
question_text: Why does the paper rise?
audio_script: I am going to show you something that contradicts your intuition. Hold a sheet of paper by its edge. Blow across the top. The paper rises. Almost everyone expects it to sink, because you are blowing on it. It rises instead. Why? Moving air has lower pressure than still air at the same height. This is Bernoulli's principle, and it is one of the most counterintuitive facts in everyday physics. The reason is energy. A fluid element moving fast has more kinetic energy than one moving slowly. If nothing else is pushing energy into the fluid, then the pressure, which is a form of energy density, must drop to compensate. Pressure plus half rho v squared plus rho g h equals a constant along a streamline. Where the speed goes up, the pressure must go down. Watch this in a venturi tube. The pipe narrows. By continuity the fluid must speed up to get through. As the fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. You can see the pressure drop directly if you stick a small vertical tube into the narrow section. The fluid rises less than it does in the wide section, because the pressure pushing it up is smaller. Every atomizer, every carburetor, every chimney, every curveball, every airplane wing leans on this same fact. The air on the curved top of a wing moves faster than the air underneath, so the pressure up there is lower, and the wing is pushed upward. Not because the wing is being sucked up. Because the ordinary pressure underneath has no counterweight above it. Fast air, low pressure. Slow air, high pressure. It is that simple and that strange.

tagline: Action at a distance becomes local action
question_text: How does one charge know another is nearby?
audio_script: I am going to show you how one charge knows that another charge is nearby. It cannot see. It cannot shout. Yet if you bring two positive charges close together, they repel. Instantly. With no visible connection between them. Newton called this action at a distance, and he hated it. He thought it was the greatest absurdity in physics. Faraday found a way out, and it is one of the great conceptual shifts in the history of science. Instead of saying that one charge reaches across space and pulls on another, say that each charge creates something in the space around it. That something is the electric field. Picture a small positive test charge that you can carry around. At every point in space, the field tells you what force that test charge would feel. Near a positive charge, the field arrows point outward, like porcupine quills. Farther away, they thin out. Double the distance and each arrow gets four times weaker, because the field falls off as one over r squared. Now place a second charge in this field. It does not need to know that the first charge exists. It only feels the field at its own location, and it responds locally. The first charge creates the field. The field travels. The second charge responds. Action at a distance has been replaced by two local events, connected by a messenger. This is why the field concept survived from Faraday to Maxwell to Einstein. A charge never reaches across space. It only changes the space right around it.

tagline: Lenz's law is energy conservation in disguise
question_text: Why does an induced current oppose its cause?
audio_script: I am going to show you that Lenz's law is not a rule you have to memorize. It is energy conservation in disguise. Move a magnet toward a coil. A current flows. Pull the magnet away. A current flows the other way. In both cases the current opposes the change. Push the magnet in, and the induced current creates a magnetic field that pushes back. Pull the magnet out, and the induced current creates a field that pulls in. Always fighting. Always resisting. Why? Here is the deep answer. Suppose the opposite. Suppose the current ran the other way. Then pushing the magnet in would pull it faster, which would induce more current, which would pull harder, which would induce still more current. Runaway. You would get energy from nothing. The universe forbids this. Lenz's law is the minus sign in Faraday's equation, and that minus sign is not decoration. It is the reason the laws of electromagnetism are consistent with energy conservation. Move a metal plate through a magnetic field, and eddy currents form inside it that resist the motion. This is magnetic braking, used on high-speed trains and roller coasters. Move a superconductor through a magnetic field, and the currents become perfect and the material floats. Lenz's law is energy conservation wearing a magnetic disguise.

tagline: Special relativity explains magnetic force
question_text: Why do parallel currents attract?
audio_script: I am going to show you that magnetism is not a separate force. Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction. They attract. This is strange. Both wires contain moving electrons, and like charges repel. So why do the wires pull together? Take the rest frame of the moving electrons inside one wire. From that frame, the other wire is not neutral. The positive ions in the other wire are moving backward, and length contraction packs them closer together. The electrons in the other wire are also moving, but at a different speed, so their spacing changes by a different amount. The net effect is a charge imbalance. A charge imbalance means an electric field. And an electric field pulls. What we call magnetism in the lab frame, an observer riding on the electrons calls electricity. Same force, different accounting. The mathematics comes out clean. The magnetic force is the electric force multiplied by v squared over c squared. It is a relativistic correction to Coulomb's law. Magnetism is not a fundamental force. It is electricity viewed from a moving frame. This is why the speed of light appears in Maxwell's equations. This is why an electric motor and a moving charge are the same physics. This is why special relativity was not a revolution that replaced electromagnetism. It was a lens that revealed electromagnetism had been one thing all along. Every magnet on your refrigerator is a relativistic artifact.

tagline: Entropy counts arrangements
question_text: Why does heat flow one way and never the other?
audio_script: I am going to show you why you cannot un-stir coffee. Put a single drop of ink into a glass of water. Stir once. The ink spreads. It keeps spreading. After a minute it is evenly distributed through the glass. It stays that way. Now try to reverse it. Try to gather all the ink molecules back into a single concentrated drop, in one small corner of the glass. You cannot. Not because the laws of mechanics forbid it. Every collision between ink and water is reversible. If you ran the movie backwards, every collision would still obey Newton's laws. Nothing about the microscopic dynamics prefers one direction over the other. But the number of ways to arrange the ink molecules so that they are all in one corner is astronomically smaller than the number of ways to arrange them so that they are spread evenly. The system evolves toward the more numerous arrangements, not because it is forced to, but because it is overwhelmingly more likely. This is entropy. The second law of thermodynamics says that in an isolated system, entropy never decreases. Not because the reverse is forbidden. Because the reverse is so improbable that you would need to wait longer than the age of the universe to see it. The universe is not marching toward disorder. It is marching toward the most numerous arrangements. Almost all of them look disordered to us.

header_title: Average Speed Is Not the Average
tagline: You cannot just average the two speeds
question_text: A jogger runs 2 km at 10 km/h then 2 km at 6 km/h. Average speed?
audio_script: Two kilometres at ten. Two at six. Average speed? The tempting answer is eight. The average of ten and six. Wrong. Average speed is total distance over total time. Time running, two over ten, is zero point two hours. Time walking, two over six, is zero point three three hours. Total time, zero point five three hours. Four over zero point five three is seven point five. Answer A. Closer to the slow speed, because more time was spent there. This is the harmonic mean. It shows up whenever you average rates.

tagline: Law of cosines in disguise
question_text: A is 10 units west. B is 5 units at 70 deg north of east. Resultant?
audio_script: A is ten units due west. B is five units at seventy degrees north of east. What is the resultant? The angle between them, taken tip to tail, is one hundred ten degrees. Use the law of cosines. R squared equals ten squared plus five squared minus two times ten times five times cosine of seventy degrees. That is one hundred plus twenty five minus one hundred times zero point three four two. Which gives ninety. The square root of ninety is about nine point five. Answer A.

tagline: Escape is only root two times orbital
question_text: What is the escape velocity from the Earth's surface?
audio_script: What speed do you need to leave the Earth and never come back? Set the kinetic energy equal to the gravitational binding energy. One half m v squared equals G M m over R. The m cancels. v equals the square root of two G M over R. G is six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven. M is five point nine eight times ten to the twenty four kilograms. R is six point three seven times ten to the sixth metres. Plug in. v is eleven point two kilometres per second. Answer B. That is about twenty five thousand miles per hour. The escape speed is the orbital speed times the square root of two. This is why the Moon has no atmosphere. Its escape speed is too low to hold on to gas molecules.

tagline: Conservation of momentum in one line
question_text: A 20 g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 500 g block. Block speed?
audio_script: A twenty gram bullet is fired at three hundred meters per second into a stationary five hundred gram block. It embeds. What is the speed of the block just after? Momentum is conserved because the collision is very fast compared to any external forces. Before. Zero point zero two times three hundred equals six kilogram meters per second. After, the combined mass is zero point five two kilograms. Six divided by zero point five two is eleven point five meters per second. Answer B. Notice that kinetic energy is not conserved. Before, nine hundred joules. After, only about thirty four. The rest went into deforming the block and heating it.

tagline: The period ignores mass and amplitude
question_text: A one metre pendulum swings. What is its period?
audio_script: A pendulum one metre long. What is its period? The formula is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Plug in L equals one, g equals nine point eight. The square root of one over nine point eight is about zero point three two. Two pi times that is about two seconds. Answer C. Notice that the period does not depend on the mass of the bob, or on the amplitude, as long as the amplitude is small. This property, called isochronism, is why pendulums were the most accurate timekeepers for three centuries.

tagline: Continuity plus Bernoulli
question_text: Water speeds up in a pipe. Does the pressure rise or fall?
audio_script: Water flows through a horizontal pipe. At point one, pressure is two times ten to the fifth pascals, speed is two meters per second. At point two, pressure is one point five times ten to the fifth pascals. What is the speed there? Bernoulli says the sum of pressure and kinetic energy density is constant along a horizontal streamline. Solve for v two. v two equals the square root of v one squared plus two times the pressure difference over rho. Pressure difference is zero point five times ten to the fifth. Two times that divided by one thousand is one hundred. Plus four. Square root of one hundred four is about ten point two. The closest answer is C, ten meters per second.

tagline: Coulomb beats gravity by ten to the thirty ninth
question_text: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton?
audio_script: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton. Both follow inverse square laws. The ratio is independent of distance. Electric force is k e squared over r squared. Gravitational force is G m e m p over r squared. Divide. The r squared cancels. k is nine times ten to the ninth. e squared is two point five six times ten to the negative thirty eight. G is six point six seven times ten to the negative eleven. The ratio comes out to two point three times ten to the thirty nine. Answer C. Electric force is two thousand billion billion billion billion times stronger. And yet gravity runs the universe, because positive and negative charges cancel on large scales and masses do not.

tagline: The period does not depend on speed
question_text: A proton at 5e6 m/s in a 0.5 T field. What is the orbital period?
audio_script: A proton moves in a magnetic field of half a tesla. What is the period of its circular orbit? The period is two pi m over q B. m for a proton is one point six seven times ten to the negative twenty seven. q is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen. B is zero point five. Plug in. Two pi times one point six seven times ten to the negative twenty seven, divided by one point six times ten to the negative nineteen times zero point five. That gives about six point six times ten to the negative eight seconds. Answer B. Notice something strange. The period does not depend on the speed of the proton. Faster protons travel in larger circles. Slower protons travel in smaller circles. But every proton completes one revolution in the same time. This is why cyclotrons work. You can keep pushing the protons with the same frequency, regardless of how fast they are going.

tagline: Time dilation at high speed
question_text: A proton at 0.99999c crosses a 100000 ly galaxy. What is the proper time?
audio_script: A proton travels at zero point nine nine nine nine nine c across the Milky Way. The galaxy is one hundred thousand light years across in its own rest frame. How much time elapses on the proton's own clock? The Lorentz factor for that speed is about three hundred sixteen. Proper time equals coordinate time divided by gamma. One hundred thousand years divided by three hundred sixteen is about four hundred fifty years. Answer A. From the proton's point of view, the galaxy is not one hundred thousand light years across. It is about three hundred twenty. The proton never breaks the speed of light. It just takes a shortcut through spacetime.

tagline: Below it
question_text: nothing
option_a: Potassium has a work function of 2.0 eV. What is the threshold wavelength?
audio_script: [{"type":"wave_pulse","id":"packet","color":"#4CC9F0"}]
orientation: Potassium has a work function of two electron volts. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject an electron? At the threshold, the energy of the photon exactly equals the work function. h c over lambda equals phi. Solve for lambda. Six point six three times ten to the negative thirty four, times three times ten to the eighth, divided by two point zero times one point six times ten to the negative nineteen. That is six point two four times ten to the negative seven metres. Answer A, six hundred twenty four nanometres. That is deep red. Longer wavelengths, in the infrared, cannot eject electrons from potassium, no matter how bright the light is. Brightness does not matter. Only frequency. This is why Einstein's photon model replaced the wave model of light.
